title: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
hook: a student loses a queen's earrings to a disguised snake king, and carries the grudge all the way to Janamejaya
tomorrow: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame

segments.voice: Yesterday the Adi Parva opened in a forest: a traveler, and a story first told at King Janamejaya's snake sacrifice. Whose story did you trace back? Day six hundred ninety-eight.

A student finishes his studies and asks his teacher what fee he can pay. The teacher sends him to ask his wife, and she names it: the earrings worn by the queen of King Paushya, brought back in time for a rite she means to wear them to. The student's name is Uttanka. He goes, and the queen gives him the earrings, with a warning: Takshaka, the king of the snakes, wants them badly. Be careful. On the road home, Uttanka sets the earrings down to wash before his prayers. When he looks up, they're gone. Today's piece of the frame is how a snake king made an enemy.
screen: `A STUDENT'S FEE.` → `A QUEEN'S EARRINGS.` → `SET DOWN, AND GONE.`

segments.voice: The thief was a wandering beggar, and as Uttanka chases him, the beggar drops the disguise. It's Takshaka. He slips into a hole in the earth, down into the world of the snakes, and Uttanka follows him. What happens down there reads like a dream. Uttanka praises the snakes in verses, and still doesn't get the earrings back. He sees two women at a loom, weaving with black and white threads. He sees a wheel turned by boys, and a man with a horse. The man tells him to blow into the horse, and when he does, smoke and fire pour through the snake world, and a frightened Takshaka hands the earrings back. When Uttanka gets home, his teacher explains the figures he saw as gods and powers; the horse, he says, was Agni, fire itself. Uttanka pays his fee in time. Done, you'd think. But Uttanka doesn't let it go. He travels to the capital, to King Janamejaya, and tells the king: Takshaka is the one who killed your father. Avenge him. Now look at what the Adi Parva is doing. The snake sacrifice doesn't begin with the king's grief alone. It begins with a student's grudge, carried a long way and set beside someone else's wound. Uttanka has his own score with Takshaka, and he finds a king with a bigger one. That's a question the frame keeps raising: how does anger spread? Not always from the person who was hurt. Sometimes from the one standing next to them, saying, you shouldn't let this go. Janamejaya turns to his ministers and asks how his father died. Their answer comes in a few days. First, the frame turns aside, and a snake speaks up for mercy.
screen: `THE BEGGAR WAS TAKSHAKA.` · `DOWN INTO THE SNAKE WORLD.` · `SMOKE AND FIRE; THE EARRINGS BACK.` · `UTTANKA GOES TO THE KING.` · then, large: `HOW DOES ANGER SPREAD?`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Bring to mind a grudge you've been handed. Not one that began with you: one someone else passed you. A family feud. A coworker's complaint about someone you barely know. An old story about a whole group of people. Just notice it, set down in front of you, the way Uttanka set the earrings on the ground. Whose was it first? Did you choose to carry it? You don't have to put it down today. Just see it clearly for a minute, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Adi Parva. The opening book, where a student's grudge against a snake king reaches a king's ear.
Your line: how does anger spread? Today, when someone hands you their anger, notice it before you pick it up. Day six hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Paying a teacher's fee at the end of study, guru dakshina, is a custom some Hindu students still keep, often as a gift or a service the teacher asks for. In the Adi Parva, Uttanka's journey ends at Janamejaya's court, and that is where the snake sacrifice begins to be urged.

fork.setup: you're Uttanka. you got the earrings back and paid your teacher. the snake king who robbed you is still out there. what do you do?
options: let it go; the fee is paid.
go to King Janamejaya and urge revenge.
go back down and fight Takshaka alone.
fork.reveal: he goes to the king and tells him Takshaka killed his father. a student's grudge helps light a king's sacrifice.

trapdoor: what you thought: the snake sacrifice is one king's grief.
what it means: it's urged on by Uttanka, a student with his own grudge against Takshaka.
what a scholar hears: the Paushya section: the earrings, the journey below the earth, and Uttanka's appeal to Janamejaya.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Paushya Parva (Uttanka and the earrings; his appeal to Janamejaya)

notes: All paraphrase (Ganguli is not on the validator's list).

Check the details of Uttanka's underworld journey: the weaving women with black and white threads, the wheel turned by boys, the man with the horse, and the teacher's later explanation. The script names only the horse as Agni; confirm that identification in Ganguli.
The script says Uttanka set the earrings down to wash before prayers; Ganguli has him set them down to perform ablutions. Confirm.
The interpretive point (the sacrifice urged on by a student's grudge) is the script's framing.
The episode of Sarama's curse on Janamejaya, which opens the Paushya section, is left out.
